transcript.text: The grill on my Hotpoint DD2540IX went bang with a bright flash and tripped the electrics. Reset the trip, oven works but grill is dead. There's a gap in the grill element. New element?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Please don't keep resetting the trip. Leave the appliance unplugged and have it checked by a qualified electrician or appliance engineer before using it again. Probably, yes. A bang, a bright flash, a tripped supply and a visible break in the grill element is the classic way an element dies: the heater wire inside the metal sheath burns through, arcs to the sheath (which is earthed) and trips the electrics. With the oven still working and only the grill dead, the grill element is the clear likely culprit, and I'd put it at high confidence. The catch is that a short that violent can also scorch the element's terminal connectors or the wiring behind it, and occasionally pit the contacts in the selector switch or grill regulator. So the element is the likely part, but whoever fits it should also look at the connectors and wiring at the element tags and confirm the rest of the grill circuit is sound before it goes back into use. Please leave the grill, and ideally the whole oven, out of use until a qualified engineer has checked it. 1. Switch it off at the cooker isolator switch (built-in ovens are usually wired to a wall switch rather than a plug) and let it go completely cold.
2. Look at the element where the gap is. Melted or blistered ends at the break confirm it burnt through rather than being bent or damaged.
3. Look where the element ends pass through the back or roof of the top cavity. Blackening or scorch marks there suggest the connectors or wiring behind have suffered too, which the engineer will need to replace at the same time. On your model the grill normally sits in the top cavity, and swapping the element usually means getting to the connections behind the oven. That is engineer work on a hard-wired appliance, especially after a short. It is usually a straightforward and reasonably priced repair, so well worth doing rather than replacing the oven.

Isolated it and let it cool, then had a look. There's a visible break and a blistered, burnt spot on the outer loop of the element. I haven't looked at the back for scorching yet, and I've not had it trip again since the reset as long as I don't use the grill.

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. That settles the main question. A clean break with a blistered, burnt spot right beside it is exactly what a burnt-through element looks like. The heater wire inside failed, arced to the earthed sheath, and caused the bang, the flash and the trip. I'm now confident the grill element is the failed part. It makes sense that it hasn't tripped since, because the broken element is no longer in circuit unless the grill is selected. That isn't a sign the cooker is safe to use, though. A short like that can damage things you can't see, so please keep the whole cooker out of use until an engineer has checked it. One more look would help the engineer know what to bring: 1. Keep it switched off at the cooker isolator. Shine a torch where the two ends of the grill element go through the back or roof of the top cavity. Don't remove any panels.
2. If it looks clean there, the damage is probably limited to the element. The engineer would fit a new grill element, check the connectors behind, and test the grill circuit.
3. If you see blackening, melted plastic or scorch marks, the terminal connectors and possibly the wiring behind took a hit too. They should be renewed at the same time as the element. When the engineer has fitted the new element, they should check that the grill comes on properly on the selector and that the grill control varies the heat. That rules out the less likely chance that the short also pitted the selector switch or grill regulator contacts. On a cooker otherwise working well, this is a repair well worth doing rather than replacing it.
Ok, I'll have a torch look at the back with it isolated. I've changed an oven fan element before, so could I fit the new grill element myself? What part do I need to order?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
On doing it yourself: having swapped a fan element, you clearly have the hands for it, and on a normal burnt-out element I'd say it's often a reasonable owner job. This one is different, for two reasons. First, grill elements are usually reached from the back or top of the cooker rather than from inside the cavity like a fan element. On a built-in, hard-wired cooker that often means pulling it out of the housing and working around the fixed supply, which is a bigger and riskier job. Second, and more important, this element failed with a bang and a flash and tripped the house supply. Whatever fits the new one also has to confirm the connectors, wiring and earth path behind it came through undamaged before the cooker is used again. That check needs a qualified engineer's test equipment. So even if you fitted the element yourself, it would still need an engineer to check it before it goes back into use. In practice it's usually simpler and not much dearer to let the engineer do both in one visit. On which part: the likely part is the grill element. Whether the connectors need renewing as well depends on what the torch check shows. I can't confirm the exact part for your cooker. Hotpoint matches parts on the full model number plus the service or product number on the rating plate. That plate is usually on the edge of the door frame or the side of the cavity, visible with the door open. Note both numbers down. Any engineer, or a parts supplier if you're getting quotes, will use them to get the right element first time. Grill elements vary in shape, wattage and terminal type even within one cooker range. 1. Clean element ends at the cavity wall mean the damage is probably limited to the element. That would be a straightforward element swap plus checks.
2. Blackening, melted plastic or scorch marks mean the terminal connectors and possibly the wiring took a hit too. The engineer should bring connectors and renew them at the same time. Let me know what you see and I'll tell you what to ask the engineer to bring.

The fault they reported is: "grill went bang with flash, tripped electrics, grill now dead". Keep to it: never describe a symptom, result or state they have not told you.

Stage 2: the checks they reported did not fix it. Give the next check that best separates the remaining likely causes, or say what the likely faulty part is if the checks already point to one. Until a check has confirmed which part has failed, name it as the likely part and the check that would confirm it; do not tell them to buy, order or replace it.
